links.note: What the pictures share is traditional hand-craft work - the heritage-of-crafts concept, not the pot-making steps (682)
Handmade versus machine-made, answered on cultural significance and the artisan's touch - the value of traditional craft

The real question in the tail is whether pot making is easy, answered by walking the steps - trekking for clay, pounding, shaping without collapse; that is 682, not 684, since no persistence of Sentila's is in view
'Tradition did not belong to any individual' is the council's argument that skills belong to the community and must be passed on - 688's wording; 683 would be heritage in general
The sentence prompts are used to voice Sentila and Arenla clearing the air ('I was afraid to tell you', 'I wish you had told me earlier') - the hidden tension being resolved
Sentila as the main character - she is the figure 684 is written around, the learner who persists
Her passion is pot making and it is 'hidden' precisely because her mother wants weaving - the expectation-versus-passion conflict
She watches the expert potters keenly - learning by observation, 686 exactly
She hides her desire - the unspoken clash with what her family expects of her; 689 covers the tension once it is out and resolved
Arenla discourages her because the craft is messy and exhausting - the mother's objection at the heart of 685
Trekking long distances for clay is the first step of the process 682 lists
Arenla wanted her to learn handloom weaving - the family expectation named in 685's description
How Arenla sells weaving as a profitable job - her case for the alternative she prefers
Weaving's handsome income - the same argument the mother uses against pottery
Weaving as a clean job, set against messy pottery - the mother's preference, so 685
The village council notices the skill is not being taught - the community's claim on the craft
The council's warning to Mesoba that skills belong to the people and must be passed to the next generation - 688 in full
Onula cannot tell the daughter's pots from the mother's - the success that follows the mother finally teaching her, which is the resolution 689 names; 687 is Onula's own mentoring
The council summoned the father - the community body acting on the duty to transmit the craft
The gentle nature of the council's warning - still an item about the community's insistence
Passing on knowledge as a cultural duty - the obligation 688 describes
The father's supportiveness is the counterweight inside the family that moves the conflict towards resolution; 685 is specifically the mother's weaving expectation
Mesoba defends his daughter's potential and promises support - a family-dynamics item, where 688 would be the council's side of the scene
Council and husband together pressure Arenla - the push that ends the standoff with her daughter
Clay pounded inside bamboo cylinders - the pounding step of the process; 693 is for naming the tools and terms themselves
Asks which tool shapes the clay, with other tools as distractors - a pottery-terminology item, and 'spatula' is listed in 693
The specific rhythm shaping demands - how the shaping step is performed, so the process concept
She turns clumsy under her mother's strict eyes - the mother-daughter tension, not the general failure-and-persistence of 684
Discouraged, frustrated and ashamed after repeated failure - the failures 684 says she persists through
Onula's arrival as the turning point - the mentor concept
Onula as thoughtful and generous - the qualities that make her the guide in 687
Onula noticing her struggling wearily - the mentor's attentiveness that precedes her help
Onula recognises a lack of confidence rather than of tools - the mentor's diagnosis
She creates a calm rather than critical environment - the encouragement half of 687
Gentle words of reassurance - 687's patient encouragement
Onula patiently demonstrating technique, contrasted with Arenla's strictness - the teaching style at the centre of 687
Her support finally lets Sentila relax - the effect of the mentoring
